extracted.intended_audience: students, playwrights, and scholars studying dramatic theory and the craft of tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (plot, character, diction, song, scenery, and related formal requirements) based on Aristotle's Poetics. Emphasises plot unity, magnitude, catharsis, and the six constituent parts of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament; the form of action is such as to effect a proper purgation (catharsis) of pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key components: seriousness, completeness (a whole), sufficient magnitude, embellished language (rhythm, harmony, song), and the emotional aim of producing pity and fear leading to catharsis. Evaluate works by whether they meet each element and produce the intended emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality — namely, Plot, Character, Thought, Diction, Scenery, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These parts function as follows: two constitute the medium of imitation, one the manner, and three the objects of imitation. Use this list as a checklist when composing or assessing a tragedy: ensure each part is present and integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot (mythos) is the imitation of the action — i.e., the arrangement of the incidents — and is the first principle and the soul of a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is the most important determinant of tragic quality; incidents and their artistic construction are the end of tragedy. A well-constructed plot with effective incidents will often produce stronger tragic effect than superior character-delineation or diction alone. Playwrights should prioritize making (crafting) plots over composing clever verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (structural unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot must imitate one whole action — it must be complete, with a beginning, middle, and end; the structural union of parts should be such that removal of any part disjoints the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot should represent one action with internal causal/probable connections so that events follow by necessity or probability. Avoid episodic sequences of incidents that lack necessary or probable connection; such episodic plots are judged inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning, Middle, End (causal sequencing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A beginning is that which does not itself follow anything by causal necessity but after which something naturally is or comes to be; an end naturally follows something and has nothing following it; a middle follows something and is followed by something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots so each part fulfils its causal place; neither begin nor end arbitrarily. Ensure transitions are motivated by probability or necessity to preserve coherence and produce the intended effects (surprise, reversal, recognition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and Length
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must be of a certain magnitude — large enough to be intelligible and beautiful, yet small enough to be embraced in one view or by memory; the proper magnitude admits a change from good fortune to bad or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pieces that are too short (appear confused) or too long (audience cannot grasp unity). For dramatic presentation, choose a span manageable for audience memory and perception; in competitions, practical time-limits may apply, but artistic theory prescribes a magnitude that lets the whole be perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time (temporal limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun (a short, bounded time): unlike Epic, which has no strict temporal limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plots that occur within a compact timeframe to maintain intensity and plausibility of causal sequence; avoid sprawling temporal expanses that undermine unity of action (unless the form intentionally permits it, as in Epic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity is of Action, not of Hero
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot does not consist in unity of the hero; a single person's life contains many actions and incidents which cannot be reduced to one action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake a single famous or complex protagonist for plot unity. Select or shape one action (one main causal arc) rather than attempting to include all notable episodes of a hero's life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility: Probability and Necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should relate what may happen — what is possible according to probability or necessity — rather than merely what has happened; events should follow plausibly from plot structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design events so they feel inevitable or highly probable within the world of the play; coincidences are effective only when they have an air of design and are connected by internal causes. This enhances the tragic wonder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plots (Peripeteia and Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are Simple when the change of fortune happens without Reversal (peripeteia) or Recognition (anagnorisis); Complex plots include reversal and/or recognition arising from the plot's internal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (with reversal and recognition) are generally superior when these moments emerge naturally from the plot's internal logic. Ensure reversals and recognitions are causally motivated, not contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Episodic Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot is 'epeisodic' when episodes succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence; such episodic plots are inferior and often result from writers stretching plots for spectacle or competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect whether each episode arises from or contributes to the central action. Remove or integrate episodes that serve only as showcases or interruptions of causal continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise and the 'Tragic Wonder'
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that surprise the audience and yet follow from one another produce the strongest tragic wonder; the effect is heightened when events seem designed rather than accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for surprises that are conditioned by the plot's internal logic. Use well-placed reversals and recognitions to produce astonishment that feels both inevitable and unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Character (second in importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that which reveals moral purpose — what a man chooses or avoids — and is secondary to plot; character determines qualities of agents but serves the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be designed to make credible choices that drive the plot. Speeches or portrayals that do not show choices (avoidances/embracings) fail to be expressive of character. A play can have tragedy without detailed character representation but cannot have tragedy without action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances — making proofs, stating general truths, or advancing reasoning within the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought to justify actions, reveal motives, and articulate universal insights. In oratory it corresponds to political or rhetorical reasoning; in drama, it helps express the intellectual shape of actions and their contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose, including metrical arrangement and choice of wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to linguistic expression and metrical choices as vehicles for meaning. While diction matters, it is subordinate to the plot; excellent diction cannot salvage a poorly constructed plot, though it enhances a good one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (melody) as chief embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song holds the chief place among the embellishments of tragedy and is part of the language-embellishment that contributes to the artifice of the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choral odes, musical elements, and lyrical passages to heighten emotional effect and structural rhythm, integrating them into the parts of the play so they reinforce plot and mood rather than distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenery (opsis) as least artistic part
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery has emotional attraction but is the least artistic and is least connected with the art of poetry; spectacular effects often depend more on stagecraft than poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on scenery to support mood and spectacle but do not substitute stage machinery for the poet's craft. Evaluate plays primarily on plot, character, thought, diction, and song; scenery is supplementary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic equipment and theatrical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Because tragic imitation implies persons acting, scenic equipment, actors, masks, prologues, and scene-painting are part of tragedy's practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, theatrical conventions (masks, number of actors, chorus, scene-painting) developed to serve the dialogue and action. Use these devices to support the dramatic imitation, ensuring they do not overshadow the plot's unity and causal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and Colloquial Measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain meters suit certain forms: iambic is the most colloquial and appropriate for dialogue; trochaic tetrameter belonged to earlier satyric form; hexameters are narrative (epic) and less colloquial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match metrical choices to dramatic function: use iambic rhythms for natural conversational speech within drama; reserve hexameter for epic narration. Let the meter arise from the nature of the imitation (colloquial vs. elevated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry aims at the Universal (not mere particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry expresses the universal (what persons of given character will do), whereas history records the particular (what Alcibiades actually did). The poet thus creates plausible types and actions rather than mere reportage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting subjects and names, aim for universality — the play should reveal general truths about human action and character. It is not necessary to stick strictly to received legends; fictitious names and events can be effective if they conform to the laws of probability and articulate universal patterns.
